items.label: A
items.critique: ''till the ogres moved in', 'Maybe we shouldn't have built so close to the ogre village', 'good luck to ya' - Nox's deadpan townsfolk humour in one-liners.

items.label: B
items.critique: Three disconnected short barks (taverns, undead, fire boots) with an item hint; flat and random in the way Nox's ambient NPCs are.

items.label: C
items.critique: 'strange and desperate times', a missing full stop, and the pointed jab about the last [Class] still missing are Westwood's tone and sloppiness.

items.label: D
items.critique: 'white as milk', 'thirty men... or ten, or a hundred, depending who's drinking' - clever, but the quest-by-quest pointers with nested names are a different writer.

items.label: E
items.critique: Each line is a compressed quest summary (wolves, the silver seal, bandits and the north gate) with names and places; too informative and too uniform for Nox's chatter.

items.label: F
items.critique: Generic warnings about trade routes and caravans and 'Young [Class]! Watch yourself' - plain, mildly stiff, Westwood's ambient rumour style.

items.label: G
items.critique: 'Hail traveler', directions to the gossip spot and a 'Chief Engineer' aside: functional, slightly bland Nox town flavour.

items.label: H
items.critique: Elided dialect ('there's leeches come up'), 'a month's takings', the tower that sees carts 'an hour off' - textured village gossip that maps one-to-one onto side quests.

items.label: I
items.critique: 'wrapped up like parcels', a bandit chief counting loot in a stolen chair: vivid, but the density of [Person] references and quest hooks gives it away.

items.label: J
items.critique: A father's horn blown to mock him, a turncoat who 'knows it stone by stone' - novelistic backstory per line, not Nox's quick quips.

tells: Every new rumour points at a specific quest with names, places and a vivid detail; Westwood's townsfolk mostly say generic, sometimes random things (taverns, undead, boots) with only one or two lines pointing anywhere.
Name density: the new lines carry two or three [Person]/[Place] slots each; Westwood's rarely more than one.

Humour: Westwood's is broad and self-deprecating ('Maybe we shouldn't have built so close to the ogre village'); the new texts' is wry and observational ('or ten, or a hundred, depending who's drinking').

Register: the new texts use dialect elisions and English rural furniture (Reeve, ford, ferry, mill boys, north gate); Westwood's uses 'Hail traveler', 'Young [Class]!', 'good luck to ya' and exclamation marks.
Polish: Westwood's lines include small slips (a missing full stop) and flat functional sentences; the new ones are uniformly polished and evenly weighted.
